claim: Working memory has a limited capacity of 3−4 objects.
source: Working memory (WM) has a limited capacity of 3−4 objects (Luck and Vogel, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Luck and Vogel, 1997.

claim: Working memory is comprised of sensory storage and central executive control for manipulating stored information and supporting preparation of a contingent response.
source: Working memory (WM) has a limited capacity of 3−4 objects (Luck and Vogel, 1997) and is comprised of sensory storage and central executive control for manipulating the stored information and supporting the preparation of a contingent response (Baddeley, 1996; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Sreenivasan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baddeley, 1996; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Sreenivasan et al., 2014.

claim: Visual and fronto-parietal brain areas exhibit enhanced neuronal activity levels during memory maintenance in monkey single- and multi-unit recordings.
source: During visual WM (VWM) maintenance, these functions are achieved in visual and fronto-parietal (FP) brain areas, which exhibit enhanced neuronal activity levels during memory maintenance in both monkey single- and multi-unit recordings (Buschman et al., 2011; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Siegel et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to monkey recording studies.

claim: Visual and fronto-parietal brain areas exhibit enhanced neuronal activity levels during memory maintenance in functional MRI of humans.
source: During visual WM (VWM) maintenance, these functions are achieved in visual and fronto-parietal (FP) brain areas, which exhibit enhanced neuronal activity levels during memory maintenance in both monkey single- and multi-unit recordings (Buschman et al., 2011; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Siegel et al., 2009) and functional MRI (fMRI) of humans (Munk et al., 2002; Pessoa et al., 2002; Todd and Marois, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Visual cortex is responsible for the processing of visual information and its maintenance in VWM.
source: While the visual cortex is responsible for the processing of visual information and its maintenance in VWM (Riggall and Postle, 2012; Emrich et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Riggall and Postle, 2012; Emrich et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2013.

claim: Lateral prefrontal cortex is thought to regulate VWM maintenance, represent goals and rules, and govern response selection.
source: lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) is thought to regulate VWM maintenance, represent goals and rules, and govern response selection (Miller and Cohen, 2001; Rowe et al., 2000; Sreenivasan et al., 2014; Markowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller and Cohen, 2001; Rowe et al., 2000; Sreenivasan et al., 2014; Markowitz et al., 2015.

claim: VWM functions in primate prefrontal cortex are achieved in multiple dissociable networks.
source: Recent studies show that even in primate prefrontal cortex, these VWM functions are achieved in multiple dissociable networks (Markowitz et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Markowitz et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016.

claim: Phase synchronization is a mechanism for integrating anatomically distributed processing and regulating communication between distant assemblies.
source: Phase synchronization (PS) is a mechanism for integrating anatomically distributed processing and regulating the communication between distant assemblies (Singer, 1999; Fries, 2005, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singer, 1999; Fries, 2005, 2015.

claim: In macaque cortical recordings, inter-areal phase synchronization in beta and gamma frequency bands is enhanced by the maintenance of visual information in VWM.
source: Macaque cortical recordings have shown that in beta- (β, 15–30 Hz) and gamma- (γ, 30−90 Hz) frequency bands, inter-areal PS is indeed enhanced by the maintenance of visual information in VWM and it has been suggested to support the maintenance of VWM content (Siegel et al., 2009; Salazar et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to macaque recording studies.

claim: VWM involves large-scale β- and γ-band phase synchronization in visual and parietal regions.
source: Using MEG and EEG, source-localization, and network analyses (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009), we observed that VWM involves large-scale β- and γ-band PS in the visual and parietal regions as in invasive LFP recordings from monkeys, but also high-alpha(α)-band (11–14 Hz) synchronization in fronto-parietal areas (Palva et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior MEG/EEG study.

claim: VWM involves high-alpha-band synchronization in fronto-parietal areas.
source: Using MEG and EEG, source-localization, and network analyses (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009), we observed that VWM involves large-scale β- and γ-band PS in the visual and parietal regions as in invasive LFP recordings from monkeys, but also high-alpha(α)-band (11–14 Hz) synchronization in fronto-parietal areas (Palva et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior MEG/EEG study.

claim: β- and γ-band synchronization underlies the maintenance and integration of visual information while high-α-band synchronization supports the coordination of processing among brain regions serving attentional and central executive control.
source: This anatomical pattern suggests a putative functional division where β- and γ-band synchronization underlies the maintenance and integration of visual information while the high-α-band synchronization supports the coordination of processing among brain regions serving attentional and central executive control.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical pattern of synchronization observed in the authors' prior study.

claim: Human intracranial EEG data have revealed long-range phase-synchronization in theta, beta, and gamma bands in hippocampal memory circuits.
source: Likewise in MEG, also human intracranial EEG (iEEG) data have revealed long-range phase-synchronization in theta (θ, 4–8 Hz), β, and γ bands in hippocampal memory circuits (Fell et al., 2001; Axmacher et al., 2008; Burke et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to human iEEG studies.

claim: The amplitudes of both β- and γ-band oscillations are positively correlated with VWM task performance and individual capacity limits.
source: The amplitudes of both β- and γ-band oscillations are positively correlated with the task performance and individual capacity limits (Sauseng et al., 2009; Palva et al., 2011; Roux et al., 2012; Honkanen et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on oscillation amplitudes and VWM performance.

claim: β- and γ-band oscillations are thought to support the neuronal representations of VWM contents.
source: The amplitudes of both β- and γ-band oscillations are positively correlated with the task performance and individual capacity limits (Sauseng et al., 2009; Palva et al., 2011; Roux et al., 2012; Honkanen et al., 2015) and thought to support the neuronal representations of VWM contents (Tallon-Baudry et al., 1998; Honkanen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tallon-Baudry et al., 1998; Honkanen et al., 2015.

claim: The plateau of load-dependent strengthening in α-frequency band amplitudes during VWM is negatively correlated with individual VWM capacity.
source: In contrast, the plateau of load-dependent strengthening in α-frequency band amplitudes during VWM is negatively correlated with the individual VWM capacity (Palva et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Palva et al., 2011.

claim: α oscillations are stronger for distractors than memorized items.
source: α oscillations are stronger for distractors than memorized items (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012; Park et al., 2014.

claim: θ and/or α oscillations underlie the attentional functions of VWM by facilitating the processing of relevant and/or by suppressing irrelevant information.
source: Together with a large body of other evidence (Palva and Palva, 2007; Buffalo et al., 2011; Saalmann et al., 2012; Haegens et al., 2015), these findings suggest that θ and/or α oscillations underlie the attentional functions of VWM by facilitating the processing of relevant and/or by suppressing irrelevant information (Jensen et al., 2014; Palva and Palva, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on α oscillations and attention.

claim: Phase amplitude coupling has been suggested to underlie cross-frequency integration.
source: Phase amplitude coupling (PAC) is one form of CFC that has been suggested to underlie cross-frequency integration (Palva et al., 2005; Palva and Palva, 2007; Sirota et al., 2008; Canolty and Knight, 2010; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on PAC.

claim: During VWM maintenance, γ oscillation amplitudes are coupled to θ phase via PAC in cortical recordings.
source: Prior studies have shown that during VWM maintenance, γ oscillation amplitudes are coupled to θ phase via PAC in cortical (Sauseng et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2009) and hippocampal recordings (Axmacher et al., 2010; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to cortical and hippocampal recording studies.

claim: PAC is independent of the phase of the fast oscillations and hence cannot promote a consistent temporal and spike-time relationship between the slow and fast oscillations.
source: However, PAC is independent of the phase of the fast oscillations and hence cannot promote a consistent temporal and spike-time relationship between the slow and fast oscillations (Palva et al., 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Palva and Palva, 2012), which are essential in the regulation of neuronal communication (Singer, 1999; Fries, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on PAC and neuronal communication.

claim: n:m-cross-frequency phase synchrony is a form of CFC that indicates direct phase coupling of the slow and fast oscillations.
source: In contrast to PAC, n:m-cross-frequency phase synchrony (CFS) (Tass et al., 1998; Palva et al., 2005; Palva and Palva, 2007) is a form of CFC that indicates direct phase coupling of the slow and fast oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies defining CFS.

claim: CFS could mechanistically underlie the cross-frequency integration of synchronized networks at the temporal resolution of the faster oscillation through coordination of consistent spike timing relationships between the oscillations.
source: CFS could thus mechanistically underlie the cross-frequency integration of synchronized networks at the temporal resolution of the faster oscillation (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Palva and Palva, 2012) through coordination of consistent spike timing relationships between the oscillations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations to Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Palva and Palva, 2012.

claim: In CFS, the ratio of high and low frequencies is defined by the integers n and m so that n∙fhigh = m∙flow.
source: In CFS, the ratio of high (fhigh) and low (flow) frequencies is defined by the integers n and m so that n∙fhigh = m∙flow.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about CFS.

claim: CFS has been observed in resting-state in humans.
source: In humans, CFS has been observed in resting-state (Nikulin and Brismar, 2006) and VWM tasks among EEG sensors (Schack et al., 2005; Hamidi et al., 2009; Sauseng et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nikulin and Brismar, 2006.

claim: CFS has been observed in VWM tasks among EEG sensors in humans.
source: In humans, CFS has been observed in resting-state (Nikulin and Brismar, 2006) and VWM tasks among EEG sensors (Schack et al., 2005; Hamidi et al., 2009; Sauseng et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schack et al., 2005; Hamidi et al., 2009; Sauseng et al., 2009.

claim: CFS has been observed in a mental calculation WM task among MEG sensors.
source: and in a mental calculation WM task among MEG sensors (Palva et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Palva et al., 2005.

claim: Prior sensor-level CFS studies leave the cortical sources of CFS as well as its functional significance unclear.
source: However, being limited to the sensor level, these studies leave the cortical sources of CFS as well as its functional significance unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of sensor-level studies.

claim: A recent study using intracranial EEG reported behaviorally significant θ:β and θ:γ CFS during VWM in human hippocampus using a serial Stenberg task.
source: A recent study using intracranial EEG (iEEG) also reported behaviorally significant θ:β and θ:γ CFS during VWM in human hippocampus using a serial Stenberg task (Chaieb et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chaieb et al., 2015.

claim: CFS has been observed in neocortical microcircuits in rats.
source: Additionally, CFS has also been observed in the neocortical (Roopun et al., 2008) and hippocampal (Belluscio et al., 2012) microcircuits in rats.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Roopun et al., 2008.

claim: CFS has been observed in hippocampal microcircuits in rats.
source: Additionally, CFS has also been observed in the neocortical (Roopun et al., 2008) and hippocampal (Belluscio et al., 2012) microcircuits in rats.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Belluscio et al., 2012.

claim: CFS was load-dependently enhanced between theta and alpha–gamma oscillations during VWM maintenance among visual, FP, and dorsal attention systems.
source: Using concurrent magneto- and electroencephalography, we found that CFS was load-dependently enhanced between theta and alpha–gamma and between alpha and beta-gamma oscillations during VWM maintenance among visual, FP, and dorsal attention (DA) systems.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CFS was load-dependently enhanced between alpha and beta-gamma oscillations during VWM maintenance among visual, FP, and dorsal attention systems.
source: Using concurrent magneto- and electroencephalography, we found that CFS was load-dependently enhanced between theta and alpha–gamma and between alpha and beta-gamma oscillations during VWM maintenance among visual, FP, and dorsal attention (DA) systems.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CFS connected the hubs of within-frequency-synchronized networks.
source: CFS also connected the hubs of within-frequency-synchronized networks and its strength predicted individual VWM capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The strength of CFS predicted individual VWM capacity.
source: CFS also connected the hubs of within-frequency-synchronized networks and its strength predicted individual VWM capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hit rate decreased as a function of VWM load but remained above chance level for the highest load of six objects.
source: The hit rate (HR) decreased as a function of VWM load but remained above chance level for the highest load of six objects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CFS between middle frontal sulcus and occipital pole as well as 1:1 α and γ band synchronization in separate networks were strengthened during VWM retention in single trials.
source: We then quantified n:m CFS (Palva et al., 2005; Tass et al., 1998) and 1:1 synchronization with the phase-locking value (PLV) in sliding time windows (Figure 2d) and found in single trials that CFS between these regions as well as 1:1 α and γ band synchronization in separate networks were strengthened during VWM retention.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-trial data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: CFS of low-θ and low-α oscillations with their corresponding higher frequency bands was concurrently suppressed below baseline levels.
source: In contrast, CFS of low-θ (3–4 Hz) and low-α (7−10 Hz) oscillations with their corresponding higher frequency bands was concurrently suppressed below baseline levels (Figure 3b; external source data 1, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3b and external source data 1.

claim: CFS among cortical oscillations is both up- and down-regulated dynamically by VWM maintenance.
source: These data hence show that CFS among cortical oscillations is both up- and down-regulated dynamically by VWM maintenance.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed up- and down-regulation of CFS.

claim: The harmonic consistency of CFS across frequency ratios was significant for the enhanced CFS in high-θ and high-α bands.
source: We quantified this by comparing the harmonic consistency of CFS across frequency ratios against surrogate data (see Materials and methods) and found this consistency to be significant for the enhanced CFS in high-θ and high-α bands and for the suppressed CFS in the low-α band (Figure 3a and b, p < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The harmonic consistency of CFS across frequency ratios was significant for the suppressed CFS in the low-α band.
source: We quantified this by comparing the harmonic consistency of CFS across frequency ratios against surrogate data (see Materials and methods) and found this consistency to be significant for the enhanced CFS in high-θ and high-α bands and for the suppressed CFS in the low-α band (Figure 3a and b, p < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: θ and high-α oscillations are systematically phase coupled with β and γ networks for which they provide temporal framing across a range of frequency ratios.
source: These data thus suggest that θ and high-α oscillations are systematically phase coupled with β and γ networks for which they thus provide temporal framing across a range of frequency ratios.
evidence: This is an inference from the harmonic consistency findings.

claim: CFS between the high-α-band consistent frequency pairs was positively correlated with memory load.
source: We found that CFS between the high-α-band consistent frequency pairs was positively correlated with memory load (Spearman's rank correlation test, α = 0.05, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Load condition.

claim: For θ-consistent CFS, VWM load-dependent modulations were weak.
source: while for θ-consistent CFS, VWM load-dependent modulations were weak.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Load condition.

claim: Low-α consistent CFS was negatively correlated with VWM load.
source: Further, low-α consistent CFS was negatively correlated with VWM load (Figure 3c–d; external source data 1, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c-d and external source data 1.

claim: Neither the leave-one-out nor the effect size masks or their combined effects led to marked changes in the overall patterns of Mean or Load condition findings.
source: Neither the leave-one-out (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a) nor the effect size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) masks or their combined effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c) led to marked changes in the overall patterns of Mean or Load (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d–f) condition findings.
evidence: The claim is supported by control analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The present findings are robust despite the smallish sample size and cannot be attributable to any single subject.
source: The present findings are thus robust despite the smallish sample size and cannot be attributable to any single subject.
evidence: This is an inference from the leave-one-out and effect size analyses.

claim: The observed CFS changes were much larger than those predicted by changes in SNR in both the Mean and Load conditions.
source: However, we did not find any systematic relationship between SNR and CFS, and observed that as in similar prior analyses for 1:1 PS (Palva et al., 2010), the observed CFS changes were much larger than those predicted by changes in SNR in both the Mean (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and Load (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by SNR control analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and 5.

claim: The task effects on oscillation amplitudes were either insignificantly correlated with the CFS effects or explained only a small fraction of the variance in CFS PLV.
source: In line with the prior findings, we found that the task effects on oscillation amplitudes were either insignificantly correlated with the CFS effects or, in the few ratio-frequency pairs where a significant correlation was observed, explained only a small fraction of the variance in CFS PLV (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by amplitude correlation analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The Mean- and Load-condition CFS effects are unlikely to be explained by concurrent changes in SNR.
source: Overall, the pattern of these correlations was far from the pattern of CFS and hence the Mean- and Load-condition CFS effects are unlikely to be explained by concurrent changes in SNR.
evidence: This is an inference from the amplitude correlation analyses.

claim: The observed pattern of CF amplitude correlations was saliently distinct from CFS.
source: However, the observed pattern of CF amplitude correlations was saliently distinct from CFS (Figure 3—figure supplement 7; external source data 2, Siebenhühner et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7 and external source data 2.

claim: Within each frequency-ratio pair, the vast majority of significant CFS connections did not exhibit significant amplitude-amplitude coupling.
source: and within each frequency-ratio pair, the vast majority of significant CFS connections did not exhibit significant amplitude-amplitude coupling (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: Changes in SNR or in waveform non-sinusoidalities could not have contributed significantly to the observations of CFS in this study.
source: These analyses thus rule out the possibility that changes in SNR or in waveform non-sinusoidalities could have contributed significantly to the observations of CFS in this study.
evidence: This is an inference from the control analyses for SNR and amplitude correlations.

claim: LF network hubs for θ-harmonic networks were found mainly in the fronto-parietal, dorsal, and ventral attention systems.
source: LF network hubs, i.e., areas wherein the θ oscillations were coupled with α−γ oscillations elsewhere, were found mainly in the fronto-parietal (FP), dorsal (DA), and ventral (VA) attention systems and included the right-hemispheric middle frontal gyrus and sulcus (mFG, mFS), intraparietal sulcus (intPS), and bilateral inferior parietal gyri (iPG) (see large circles in Figure 4a, left; external source data 3, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4a and external source data 3.

claim: HF hubs for θ-harmonic networks were observed in the DA system, SM system, and DM system.
source: HF hubs, i.e., loci where α−γ oscillations were predominantly coupled with θ elsewhere, were observed in the DA system, namely in the left inferior precentral sulcus (iprCS), right superior parietal gyrus (sPG), and intPS as well as in postcentral sulcus and gyrus (poCS/G) of the sensorimotor system (SM) and superior frontal gyrus (sFG) of the default-mode (DM) system (Figure 4a, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4a.

claim: For high-α-CFS networks, LF (high-α) hubs were observed in the right-hemispheric iPG, mFS, and iFS in the FP system and in bilateral sFG, right superior frontal sulcus (sFS), and inferior temporal gyrus (iTG) in the DM system.
source: For the CFS between high-α and γ, in networks with ratios 1:3−1:9, we observed LF (high-α) hubs in the right-hemispheric iPG, mFS, and iFS in the FP system (see blue hubs in Figure 4b, left panel) and in bilateral sFG, right superior frontal sulcus (sFS), and inferior temporal gyrus (iTG) in the DM system.
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The FP α-hubs were bilaterally and strongly connected to γ oscillations in the visual cortex.
source: Among other targets, the FP α-hubs were bilaterally and strongly connected to γ oscillations in the visual cortex (see dashed line ends of red FP-Vis connections in Figure 4b, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The HF (γ) hubs for high-α-CFS included mFG and mFS (FP), bilateral iprCS and left intPS in the DA system and the right-hemispheric cuneus (CN) and superior occipital gyrus (SOG) in the visual system.
source: The HF (here, γ) hubs included mFG and mFS (FP), bilateral iprCS and left intPS in the DA system and, importantly, the right-hemispheric cuneus (CN) and superior occipital gyrus (SOG) in the visual system.
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Visual system γ hubs were connected to high-α-oscillations in LPFC and with left-hemispheric posterior parietal cortex and visual system.
source: These visual system γ hubs were connected to high-α-oscillations in LPFC and with left-hemispheric posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and visual system (Figure 4b, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4b.

claim: CFS between high-α and γ connected the FP and DA internally and these attentional systems with the visual system.
source: CFS between high-α and γ hence connected the FP and DA internally and these attentional systems with the visual system.
evidence: This is an inference from the network visualization.

claim: In both the θ- and high-α-consistent CFS networks, the LF hubs were more salient in right-hemispheric FP areas while HF hubs were more prominent in bilateral DA and visual areas.
source: Moreover, in both the θ- and high-α-consistent CFS networks (see Figure 4a and b), the LF hubs were more salient in right-hemispheric FP areas while HF hubs were more prominent in bilateral DA and visual areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: 1:2 CFS connections between high-α and β oscillations were saliently localized to the SM, DA, and VA systems.
source: In contrast with the 1:3−1:9 α:γ CFS, 1:2 CFS connections between high-α and β oscillations were saliently localized to the SM, DA, and VA systems (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; external source data 5, Siebenhühner et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and external source data 5.

claim: The differences between α:β and α:γ CFS suggest that they may underlie functionally distinct CFC.
source: The differences between α:β and α:γ CFS suggest that they may underlie functionally distinct CFC.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed differences in network localization.

claim: Both LF and HF hubs for low-α consistent CFS suppression were predominantly found in the DM and SM systems.
source: We found that both LF and HF hubs were predominantly found in the DM and SM systems that are putatively task-irrelevant in VWM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; external source data 6, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and external source data 6.

claim: High-α (LF) hubs in the Load condition were mostly found in the left-hemispheric visual system, right-hemispheric FP, and in SM bilaterally.
source: High-α (LF) hubs were mostly found in the left-hemispheric visual system, right-hemispheric FP, including the mFS, and iPG, and in SM bilaterally (Figure 5; external source data 4, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 5 and external source data 4.

claim: The HF γ hubs in the Load condition were observed in areas overlapping with those of high-α hubs in the left-hemispheric visual system and in right-hemispheric mFG and sPG.
source: The HF γ hubs were observed in the areas overlapping with those of high-α hubs in the left-hemispheric visual system and in right-hemispheric mFG and sPG.
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 5.

claim: VWM retention was associated with significantly denser CFS coupling of θ-oscillations in DA, FP, visual, SM, and DM systems with α−γ oscillations in SM and DA than expected by chance.
source: The system-system connection density matrices largely corroborated the main phenomena found in the network visualizations and showed that VWM retention was associated with significantly denser CFS coupling of θ-oscillations in DA, FP, visual, SM, and DM systems with α−γ oscillations in SM and DA than expected by chance (Figure 6a, see Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: θ-oscillations in DA were also synchronized with α−γ oscillations in visual, FP, and limbic systems.
source: θ-oscillations in DA were also synchronized with α−γ oscillations in visual, FP, and limbic systems.
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis.

claim: High-α oscillations were synchronized with γ oscillations within DA, and between DA, visual, SM, and FP systems.
source: In line with the visualization of the most central connections (See Figure 4b), high-α oscillations were synchronized with γ oscillations within DA, and between DA, visual, SM, and FP systems (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In the Load condition, high-α oscillations in SM and visual systems were synchronized with γ oscillations in visual, SM, and DA systems.
source: However, in the Load condition, high-α oscillations in SM and visual systems were synchronized with γ oscillations in visual, SM, and DA systems, and conversely γ oscillations in FP with high-α oscillations in DA, limbic, and DM systems (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: 1:2 α:β CFS was strengthened in Mean and Load condition among SM and attentional systems as well as between DA and FP.
source: Further, in line with the visualization of strongest connections, 1:2 α:β CFS was strengthened in Mean and Load condition among SM and attentional systems (Figure 6d and e, cf. Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as also between DA and FP.
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6d and e.

claim: Low-α oscillations in SM, DA, FP and DM showed suppressed synchronization with β and γ oscillations in DM as well as in DA, SM and FP systems.
source: Low-α oscillations in SM, DA, FP and DM showed suppressed synchronization with β and g oscillations in DM as well as in DA, SM and FP systems (Figure 6f).
evidence: The claim is supported by system-level connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: For both the high-θ and high-α consistent CFS networks, the node degree centrality values were correlated with the corresponding centrality values of within-frequency synchronized networks.
source: We found that for both the high-θ (5−7 Hz) and high-α (11−14 Hz) consistent CFS networks, the node degree centrality values were correlated with the corresponding centrality values of within-frequency synchronized networks, (p < 0.05, corrected, Figure 7a, see Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The low-frequency CFS hubs were significantly co-localized with the hubs of the slow 1:1 networks.
source: Hence, the low-frequency CFS hubs were significantly co-localized with the hubs of he slow 1:1 networks.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation of node centralities.

claim: The correlations of high-frequency CFS hubs with those of the fast 1:1 networks were weaker but still significant for several frequency pairs.
source: The corresponding correlations of high-frequency CFS hubs with those of the fast 1:1 networks were weaker but still significant for several frequency pairs (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Shared hubs in both 1:1 α and LF-CFS networks were mFS, sFG, both angular and supramarginal parts of iPG, and precentral gyrus which were connected to their γ network targets in the visual system through CFS.
source: Shared key hubs in both 1:1 α and LF-CFS networks were mFS, sFG, both angular and supramarginal parts of iPG, and precentral gyrus (prCG) which were connected to their γ network targets in the visual system through CFS (Figure 7c, left column).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Hubs shared by low-γ band and HF-CFS were SOG and inferior temporal gyrus, which were connected with their α-network targets in LPFC and PPC.
source: Hubs shared by low-γ band and HF-CFS were SOG and inferior temporal gyrus (iTG), which were connected with their α-network targets is LPFC and PPC (Figure 7c, right column).
evidence: The claim is supported by network visualization shown in Figure 7c.

claim: High-α band network included co-localized CFS and 1:1 hubs in the FP and DA attention networks while the γ-band network included key hubs in the visual system and posterior brain areas.
source: Thus as proposed by our hypothesis, high-α band network included co-localized CFS and 1:1 hubs in the FP and DA attention networks while the γ-band network included key hubs in the visual system and posterior brain areas.
evidence: This is an inference from the network visualization.

claim: Low- and high-γ networks were not mutually significantly correlated in parcel centralities, which implies that these γ oscillations were relatively narrow-band and cannot particularly be explained by broad-band γ activities.
source: Despite both low- and high-γ networks being characterized by hubs in the visual system, they were not mutually significantly correlated in parcel centralities (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), which implies that these γ oscillations were relatively narrow-band and can not particularly be explained by broad-band γ activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: θ- and low-α-band phases were coupled with α- and β-band amplitudes at a 1:2 ratio.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, as the strongest effect, this analysis revealed that θ- and low-α-band phases were coupled with α- and β-band amplitudes at a 1:2 ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by PAC analysis.

claim: Weak coupling of the γ oscillation amplitudes with the phase of θ oscillations at frequency ratios up to 1:9 was found.
source: We also found weak coupling of the γ oscillation amplitudes with the phase of θ oscillations at frequency ratios up to 1:9 (Figure 8a; external source data 7, Siebenhühner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAC analysis shown in Figure 8a and external source data 7.

claim: In the high-α band, where prominent CFS was observed, PAC was suppressed.
source: Importantly, in the high-α band, where prominent CFS was observed, PAC was suppressed (Figure 8b).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAC analysis shown in Figure 8b.

claim: PAC and CFS are clearly distinct phenomena.
source: These data show that PAC and CFS are clearly distinct phenomena.
evidence: This is an inference from the different patterns of PAC and CFS.

claim: For low ratios the strength of high-α consistent CFS networks predicted VWM capacity.
source: We estimated the correlation (Pearson correlation test) between S and C and found that for low ratios the strength of high-α consistent CFS networks predicted (r = 0.343, p = 0.003) VWM capacity (Figure 9a, see Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9a.

claim: For the high (1:6−1:9) ratios, the individual capacity was correlated with high-θ consistent CFS.
source: For the high (1:6−1:9) ratios, the individual capacity was correlated (r = 0.376, p = 0.001) with high-θ consistent CFS (see Figure 9a).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Both the high-α:β (ratio 1:2) and high-α:low-γ (ratios 1:3−1:5) CFS were significantly correlated with VWM capacity.
source: We also tested whether the high-α low ratios observation was attributable only to 1:2 α:β coupling but found both the high-α:β (ratio 1:2, r = 0.247, p = 0.036) and high-α:low-γ (ratios 1:3−1:5, r = 0.232, p = 0.0496) to be significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: No PAC network strength correlations with individual VWM capacity exceeded the corrected significance threshold.
source: We then estimated correlations of PAC network strength with individual VWM capacity in the same manner (Figure 9c,d). However, no p values exceeded the corrected significance threshold.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9c,d.

claim: Cortical CFS is functionally significant in human VWM maintenance.
source: These data thus indicate that cortical CFS is functionally significant in the human VWM maintenance and also further reinforce the view that CFS and PAC are functionally distinct phenomena.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation of CFS with VWM capacity and the lack of such correlation for PAC.

claim: CFS and PAC are functionally distinct phenomena.
source: These data thus indicate that cortical CFS is functionally significant in the human VWM maintenance and also further reinforce the view that CFS and PAC are functionally distinct phenomena.
evidence: This is an inference from the different behavioral correlations of CFS and PAC.

claim: CFS connects slow and fast cortical oscillations across the visual, FP, and DA systems during VWM retention.
source: We found that CFS connects slow and fast cortical oscillations across the visual, FP, and DA systems during VWM retention.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The strength of CFS was dynamically up- and down-regulated, correlated with VWM task demands, and predictive of individual VWM capacity.
source: The strength of CFS was dynamically up- and down-regulated, correlated with VWM task demands, and predictive of individual VWM capacity, which show that CFS is a functionally significant cross-frequency interaction mechanism during VWM maintenance.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: CFS is a functionally significant cross-frequency interaction mechanism during VWM maintenance.
source: The strength of CFS was dynamically up- and down-regulated, correlated with VWM task demands, and predictive of individual VWM capacity, which show that CFS is a functionally significant cross-frequency interaction mechanism during VWM maintenance.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed properties of CFS.

claim: CFS may be a mechanism for coordinating neuronal processing and regulating communication among oscillatory networks at different frequencies.
source: We found solid support for each of these predictions, which shows that CFS may indeed be a mechanism for coordinating the neuronal processing and regulating communication among oscillatory networks at different frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings supporting the study's predictions.
